# Introduction

Data scientists, analysts as well as statisticians often face datasets with a large number of variables and observations. This requires not only increasing computational power, but also more efficient methods to handle high-dimensional data and make more accurate variable selection processes to improve predictions. For this purpose, different machine learning methods like decision trees or random forests have been developed. These were first introduced by @breiman1984. They also invented the term classification and regression trees (CART). Nowadays, trees and forests are commonly used procedures to build models for predictions of a variable of interest based on several input variables. They are implemented in statistical software like the R programming language with different packages.

In this paper, three different packages for R that offer solutions for random forests are analyzed. For this purpose, the two most popular packages called “randomForest” and “Ranger” were chosen while also adding “Party” to the repertoire which includes different functions for recursive partitioning. The afore-mentioned packages are benchmarked in terms of their computational performance and their prediction quality. The goal of this paper is to provide an empirically founded recommendation of a single R package to potential users. The preselection of the packages is necessary and based on research. It will be taken up in a dedicated chapter of this paper.

The paper is structured in the following way: firstly, the intuition of tree-structured models and how these are grown is described. After providing comprehension for CART, the theory behind random forests will be covered. In the "Data & Method" chapter of this paper, the structure of the study will be introduced. This is followed by providing background information on the selected R packages and reasons for pre-selecting the afore-mentioned R packages. Finally, the results will be summarized and concluded with recommendations for different use-cases of random forests.

# What is a random forest? How is a random forest structured/theory/hypotheses

# Data & method

## Organisation of the study

In line with the research question, empirical and simulated multinomial data is used while drawing on different implementations of the Random Forests algorithm to classify this data. Since the focus lies on comparing different R packages, different goodness of fit measures are considered after classification to evaluate the performance of the R packages. On the basis of the theory and the available information on the packages, it is expected that the Random Forests implementations perform similar across the different packages.

## Data preparation

For the analysis, on the one hand, empirical data is used. The data set originally stems from a project at the Colorado State University and was later donated to the UC Irvine Machine Learning Repository [@blackard]. The data set contains data on cover tree types and surrounding characteristics. In forestry, a cover tree type is determined by the most prevalent tree type in a certain forest area [@gislason2006]. Since the data set contains not only a large amount of observations but also many predictors, it is suitable for the use in the study. As the format of the data set matches the use in the study, the preparation of the data was only made on a small scale. <br><br> On the other hand, simulated data was used for which it is also aimed at arriving at a large number of observations and predictors. In the following, the simulation of the second data set is described where this study draws on the specifically for this purpose created function `gen_dataset`. To get artificial multinomial data and predictor variables, random draws from different **?probability density distributions?**, including the normal, the beta and the uniform distribution, are used. The simulated multinomial data then consists of seven different tree types, on the one hand. On the other hand, a large number of predictors is obtained. Moreover, correlations between the predictors were included in the simulation process as these are expected to be found in an empirical data set. The code generates a vector of random values between `min_cor` and `max_cor` which are both specified manually in advance. It then assigns a random index from remaining variables for each variable to create correlations. Afterwards, observations are selected based on the absolute value of the correlation. If the correlation is positive, the values of the variable are positively correlated with the chosen variable; if negative, they are negatively correlated.

## The different packages

As the focus in this study lies on comparing different R packages, a short introduction to each of the packages is needed. Each package has its own underlying philosophy. First, the *randomForest*-package is described, followed by *ranger* and lastly, the *party*-package [@hothorn2005] is introduced.

### randomForest

The package *randomForest* draws on the original algorithm described in @breiman2001 and originally published in Fortran [@breiman2002]. The type of dependent variable which is to be predicted determines whether classification or regression is performed using the random forest algorithm. In addition, various hyperparameters of the algorithm can be defined: for example, it is possible to specify how many variables are randomly selected at each split of the single trees (hyperparameter `mtry`). Moreover, mathematically interesting is the use of $\sqrt p$ as the default hyperparameter in classification. The *randomForest*-package can be regarded as one of the standard packages implementing the random forest algorithm, which is one of the reasons for using the package in this study.

### ranger

The package random forest generator (known as “Ranger”) package is an implementation for random forests with optimizations for high dimensional data in R. The developers Wright and Ziegler (2017: 2) claim to provide a package which is comparable simple to use. The package is optimized by extensive memory profiling for different types of input data. In contrast to the package Willows, Ranger is able to handle a larger number of features at the same time. As a random forest is proceeded in R, all values of all features of mtry are splitting candidates. Since the required computational power increases exponentially with added features, this is the bottleneck for many random forest packages and the developers of the ranger package focused on this problem. The ranger() function is used to grow a forest and makes use of two different algorithms for the splitting process. At first, the feature values are sorted and accessed by their index. In the second algorithm, the values are sorted and retrieved while splitting. Other than the package RandomForest, Ranger is license free and the software is open-source released which improves traceability of the functions for users on the one hand and accessible for implementation of new features by other developers on the other hand (Wright and Ziegler, 2017: 2 f.). It stands out, that the code for ranger is written in C++ and uses standard libraries only. C++ is described as a low-level language, which expresses in a machine-oriented design and more efficient use of memory (Haidl and Gorlatch, 2018). This makes parallel processing available and considerably accelerates the runtime. Besides from CART, survival trees are also supported by the ranger package.

### party

The documentation of the *party*-package states differences to the *randomForest*-package in the basic implementation, i.e. different base learners were used [@hothorn2005, p. 6]. Whereas the *randomForest*-package draws on Classification and Regression Trees (CART) to form a random forest, the *party*-package utilizes conditional inference trees designed to prevent overfitting and **?variable selection bias?** while combining statistical testing and the basic ideas of CART [@hothorn2006]. Also, the default of the hyperparameters are slightly different to the *randomForest*-package. For example, the default value of `mtry` equals $5$ while in *randomForest* $\sqrt p$ is specified.

## Cross-validation

For the cross-validation, a function `cv_rf` is created to apply classification by the Random Forests algorithm, while drawing on the methods implemented in the R packages described in section 3.3: `randomForest`, `ranger`, and `cforest`. With `cv_rf`, the models' performance based on accuracy, F1 score, and F-beta score, while also recording the computational time taken to fit each model.

By using parallelization techniques, various hyperparameter combinations (`ntree` and `mtry` are efficiently tested. The function is run across all combinations while collecting the results for further analysis.

The cross-validation is targeted at obtaining the optimal hyperparameter combinations as measured in different goodness-of-fit indicators for each type of data, empirical as well as simulated data,.

# Results

The packages show different patterns in case of the used computational time and the measurements of Goodness of Fit (GoF).

The Accuracy …

The F1-Score …

The F-Beta-Score …

The party package provides the lowest values for all used GoF. The ranger packages provides the best fit for all GoF in the most hyperparameter combinations.

The not chosen hyperparameters behind those functions could be the reason for the different behaviour in case of computational time and the GoF. There is a need for a deep dive into the functions, which can be found via CRAN for each individual package. For the function, which contains the computation itself, there is no written code in R. In case of RandomForest it is written in FORTRAN [@Breiman; Cutler (D. u.)] (programming language for formulas in engineering and scientific calculations), in case of ranger it is C++ [@Wright (2024)] and in case of party packages it is not clarified, where the actual function comes from [@Thothorn (2023)]. As a matter of fact there has to be a look at the preparation in R code. For every package there is one function behind which is checking and adjusting the hyperparameters. Afterwards this will be used as input for the function in the background, which computes the desired output.

It can be seen that the default in Randomforest, ranger and party is the same for ntree (= 500) (green marks in the imagine beneath). The number of variables used for each split for the selection mtry. The difference is mtry = floor(sqrt(ncol(x))) for RandomForest, which adjusts downward and mtry = ceiling(sqrt(nvar)) for party, which adjusts upward (orange marks in the imagine beneath). This happens in the header of the function. The ranger package does not adjust this parameter in the preparation in R – so it should happen in the C++ script, but in default mode it is also the square root of ncol(x) and will be rounded down.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("pics/Tab1.png")
```

Another important part is the hyperparameter sampsize (RandomForest), sample.fraction (ranger) and perturb (party). This parameter adjusts the fraction or number of observations to sample or draw – for classification it is set to one.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('pics/Tab2.png')
```

One major argument, why the predicted results differ is described in the cforest package [@Thothorn (2023), S.6]:

“Moreover, when predictors vary in their scale of measurement of number of categories, variable selection and computation of variable importance is biased in favor of variables with many potential cutpoints in randomForest, while in cforest unbiased trees and an adequate resampling scheme are used by default.”

This could be the one reason. Another reason inside the ranger package seems to be the adjusted seed by seed = runif(1, 0, max), which is the seed for the used C++ function.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('pics/pic1.png')
```

# Conclusion

From the point of view as a beginner it should be considered starting with easy packages, which provides good documentation and well explained hyperparameters. For this reason this paper recommends using either RandomForest itself. The RandomForest package is a direct product of Leo Breiman, which could be used as useful link between theory and practice.

For already advanced users of the randomforest it is recommended to use ranger. Ranger provides a more detailed documentation. Therefore, there is a connection and an use case for the paper itself. Here we can also increase the performance with the number of used threads – default is the available CPUs.

For a special kind of the randomforest the party package with the function cforest provides an alternative with conditional randomforests. The code for cforest inside the party packages is not well documented in comparison to the two other packages. This package seems to be in process of developing (regarding the comment above the code):

```{r, echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics('pics/pic2.png')
```

As well as the ranger package it is using the cores (but with no further information inside the code).

For further information and deep dive into the code of the actual computation of the random forest this should be regarded by someone with advanced programming skills.
